(Translation). Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I may be permitted to call the attention of the government, and particularly that of the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) upon a question of the utmost importance to the county of L'Assomption which I have the honour of representing, and to the other counties in my district. This matter also interests largely the city of Montreal.
By 63 and 64, Victoria, chapter 8, subsection 33, the government of this country granted in 1900 a subsidy of $150,000 to the Chateauguay and Northern Railway Company in the following terms:
To the Chateauguay and Northern Railway Company, for a single track standard railway bridge, with two roadways 10 feet wide, for free vehicular and foot passenger traffic, the same as upon a public highway, from Bout de L'lsle to Charlemagne, at the iunc-tion of the Ottawa and St. Lawrence rivers, $150,000.
I have no doubt that this subsidy has been paid to the company, but I do not know whether the latter have fulfilled the conditions upon which this subsidy has been granted.
Instead of constructing a single bridge connecting Bout de L'lsle to Charlemagne,

the said company, making use of an island-the Bourbon island-which was in the middle of the river, has erected two bridges, one from Bout de Isle to the southern shore of Bourbon island and the other from the northern shore of Bourbon island to Charlemagne.
The distance is twenty-five to thirty French acres which one has to travel in order to cross that intervening island has never been provided with a suitable road so as to permit the passage from one point to the other, and the numerous farmers conveying their farm produce to the city of Montreal and the travelling public in general have been obliged to travel that distance before any work had been done to put that road in order. The result was unavoidable;- that low and marshy ground was turned into a rut almost uninterrupted and often exasperatingly deep. In spite of repeated representations from all quarters, it has been impossible so far to have this unfortunate grievance redressed. The Montreal newspaper, especially ' La Patrie,' as late as last week, in an editorial, demonstrated the inconveniences to which the traveling public of Montreal and of the rural constituencies were subjected to on account of that altogether impassable road. Here is what ' La Patrie ' of the 26th March said:
The Bout de Pile Bridge.
La ' Patrie ' has already called the attention of the federal authorities upon the impassable and dangerous state of the approaches to the Bout de Pile bridge.
Thaw has set in. Loaded or pleasure vehicles, wagons, automobiles, etc., going from Bout de Pile to Charlemagne, or in the opposite direction, are in danger of getting stalled or of breaking to pieces in the deep ruts at the two ends of the bridge. It is almost impossible to pass there. And such is the situation since the bridge has been open to the public.
Upon whom rests the responsibility of making the necessary repairs ? Is it upon the Railways department or upon the Canadian Northern Company P
However it may be, it is really disgraceful to leave an 'important road as this in such a state of rack and ruin.
We do not know whether the contractors were bound to complete the embankment so as to facilitate the entrance to the bridge, or whether the government inspectors have reported. But it is incumbent upon the federal authorities to complete or have completed without delay that which has too long remained unfinished.
The member from L'Assumption shall undoubtedly renew his representations to the government at the re-opening of parliament.
The members of the city and the island of Montreal shall join with him to put a stop to that intolerable situation.
Every summer thousands of vehicles and automobiles cross the Bout <fe File bridge. If the approaches are not soon repaired, accidents will surely happen, entailing probably loss of life.

We instantly request the government to send an inspector thex-e and to have the necessary repairs made.
Last year, to prevent circulation from being altogether interrupted at that place which, had become dangerous, some people clubbed together in making ameliorations, and I had to put up some money myself towards that and the work we have done has been rather temporary, did not give a very passable road but rendered it less perilous.
And now that road is almost impassable. I think it is incumbent upon the government, who have granted leave to use that island instead of building a bridge over it, to relieve the travelling public which is suffering so much from that situation. Therefore. I humbly suggest to the hon. Minister of Railways that it is high time that redress be given to the thousands and thousands of people using that bridge, and that within the shortest delay an inspection and a report be made if need be, in order to fix the responsibilities of the subsidized company and to have it fulfilling its obligations.
Thus justice will be rendered to my constituents.

I have looked for precedents in this matter and I have not been able to find any, although I am quite sure there must be some. When this Bill was read a second time instead of it being referred to a Committee of the Whole it was referred to a special committee. Had it been referred to a Committee of the Whole, and had that committee reported, the question is put by the Speaker:	Shall the report
be concurred in; and then it is open to any member of the House to move either that it be concurred in or that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole for the purpose of amending it. True, we have not a report of the Committee of the Whole, but we have a report of the special committee, and I should think that the motion cf my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) would be that this report of the committee be con-. curred in, just the same as if it were a report of the Committee of the Whole.

When private Bills are referred to a special committee, and when that committee has reported, they come back again to the Committee of the Whole House. Even government measures have been dealt with in that way. I did not know that the point would come up, and hence I have not looked into it, but I never knew of a case in which the'report of the special committee was deemed to be an equivalent, or that it should supersede discussion in Committee of the Whole. I

True, when a private Bill is referred to a special committee, by the rules of the House the special committee may pass or reject the Bill, but a public Bill must always come back to Committee of the Whole House. The question under discussion has been very much narrowed in its scope. I refer hon. gentlemen to the report of the committee for the following citation, and I may say that Mr. McCarthy referred to there was one of the solicitors employed by the opponents of the Bill:

Do I understand that you are willing to co-operate with the promoters of the Bill, with the committee, in abolishing all the evils, if any, that result from handbook betting, the operations of pool rooms and the sending out of information by telegraph or otherwise.

All you wish to protect is

Mr. McCarthy. Is betting on the race track while the races are in operation.
Than the whole point of the discussion narrows itself down to that particular point-all that the opponents of the Bill desire is betting on the race tracks of a duly licensed association and during the meet. We may well ask ourselves why it is that the opponents of the Bill are willing that the scope of the discussion shall be so limited. In the first place, the professional gambling on the race track during the meet is the only thing that brings any revenue to the association, and, therefore, while the opponents of the Bill say they are willing to give up every thing but that) they are very much in the position of Mark Twain who' was willing to sacrifice all his wife's relations. I desire to ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether or not it does not appear to any reasonable, to any sensible, unprejudiced, unbiased man to be rather an absurd thing that while we by our Criminal Code, without any objection from any quarter, make the business of gambling a crime, w'e shall make an exception of the business of gambling on the race tracks. What good reason can there be why that which is wrong on the street or on a lot adjoining the race track should be perfectly proper and within the law when it takes place on a race track. I do not know what virtue there is in the atmosphere or in the soil or the surroundings of a race track that there makes right that which is pronounced to be wrong in every other place. The opponents of the Bill have laid down three prime, main objections. First, that the thoroughbred horse is necessary to the breeding of good horses; second, that racing is necessary to maintain the thorough!)#ed; third, that professional betting is necessary in order to maintain racing, and, fourth, (incidentally') that hoTse racing is the sport of kings and ought not to be interferred with or prohibited. We largely admit the first statement, that the thoroughbred is necessary or of advantage in the breeding of many kinds of horses. But, the second statement, that racing is necessary to maintain the thoroughbred, we will not admit, although it is admitted that the race track is one of the means that is found useful in the development of the thoroughbred horse. The third statement that professional betting is necessary to maintain racing we absolutely deny and refuse to admit. To the fourth allegation, that horse racing is the sport of kings and should not be prevented, we say it has never been the desire or intention of the promoters of the Bill to interfere with horse racing, and we do not think that the Bill, if carried into effect, will do awav with horse racing. Again, as to the first statement-and I dwell upon that for a few minutes because it has been made a very strong argument by the opponents of the Bill-let me say that the thoroughbred horse is never used for the improvement of any of the breeds of draft horses. Dr. Rutherford, the Dominion veterinary, who was examined before the committee as a witness in opposition to the Bill, stated in his evidence that the thoroughbred horse was not being used, so far as he knew, by any breeder of standard-bred horses, or by any breeder of hackney horses, either in the United States or Canada. If, then, it is admitted, as it is, even by the opponents of the Bill, that the thoroughbred horse is not used for the improvement of any of the breeds of draft horses, the standard-bred horse or the hackney horse, then surely the class of horses for which it is important to use the thoroughbred is a comparatively small and unimportant class. The evidence, then, of witnesses who came to oppose the Bill, goes to show that the race-track has been the means of lessening the value of the standard-bred horse. Dr. Rutherford, being asked as to that, said:
Men having speed tnares have brought them to the fastest stallion they could get without paying any attention whatever to the maintaining of the constitution, the conformation and the general symmetry of the horse.
Another gentleman who gave evidence before the committee in opposition to the Bill was Dr. McEachem, the. eminent veterinary surgeon of Montreal. He gave the following evidence:
Q. In breeding the standard bred for extreme speed have they not suffered in other qualities?-A. I think so. There has been a great deal of harm done to the country by breeding from standard bred horses.
Q. Now what I want to ask is whether the same thing has been proved about the thoroughbred, that in breeding the thoroughbred for extreme speed there has been a loss of other good qualities?-A. That is so. It 1 is well known in England that short races

have altered the character of the horses and there is a strong feeling in the United States and I know that the feeling exists in Canada that only heavy honed horses should be used for breeding and light boned horses should be eliminated, and it is quite proper. Speaking generally you are quite right.
When he says, 'speaking generally you are quite right1, he admits that the racetrack has been the cause of deteriorating rather than improving in many instances the thoroughbred horse. He was asked further:
Q. Do you think that the short races in Canada are a real test of proof of endurance on the part of the horses?-A. No.
Q. Then, if horse racing was to he the assistance to horse breeding here that it ought to be one would require to lengthen the races? -A. Yes, would have to breed as large and as heavy as you could get and lengthen the races.
Dr. Rutherford was asked this question :	[DOT]
Q. But talking recently to a man who seems to know a great deal about breeding horses, a lover of horses and a lover of sport, he said to me, and I thought he was very sensible in his remarks, that the present short races rnn on the running tracks of Canada are really no test or evidence of endurance upon the part of the horses engaged. What do you think about that?-A. That man is quite right.
Thus we have the testimony of the highest authorities in Canada that horse-racing has not improved and is not likely to improve either the standard-bred or the thoroughbred horse. The Hon. Mr. Fisher, Minister of Agriculture, was asked as to the necessity of the race-track, and particularly race-track gambling, to the improvement of the breed ofi horses. Inspector Duncan took the logical position that if it be a crime to bet up town, it must be equally a crime to bet with a book-maker on the race-track. Inspector Archibald gave evidence, page 217:
From that standpoint I think these places are worse in that respect than the. Woodbine. But, if you want my opinion as to whether the Woodbine, as a place for betting on horse races, in contrast with those places, is the more dangerous, I say by all means the Woodbine.
They are worse in as much as the handbooks are in operation all the year and the book-makers on the track only during the meeting. He added:
But if you want my opinion as to whether the Woodbine, as a place for betting on horse races, in contrast with those places, is the more dangerous, I say by all means the Woodbine.
Again Inspector Archibald said:
But there is an expenditure of tens of thousands of dollars at the track in place of that many cents in the city.
Q. The evil is greater in the Woodbine, you mean?-A. Yes.
Inspector Archibald was asked this question :
Not referring alone to those particular cases cited by detective Duncan, but the class of cases that come before your notice, would you say the larger number of them arise from betting on the race-track, or does a larger proportion of them come from betting with the hand-book men up town ?-A. By long odds the larger proportion from the Woodbine; no question about that.

Mr. Batt gave his evidence as to the comparative evils resulting from the betting on the tracks and the hand-book men up town:
Q. Now as to making a comparison between the harm that comes or that follows from betting with the book-makers and the harm that comes from the practice of betting with the hand-book men, which do you consider the greatest evil, which brings the worse results?-A. Betting with the hand-book or on the track?
Q. Yes, which ruins the most men?-A. The track.
Q. There is no doubt at all of that in your mind?-A. I know it, yes, because a man will go to the hand-book and will bet $5 or 50 cents or $2 and that is all he will bet that day. A man will go to the track and will take $300 or $200 or $500 with him, and he will loose every cent he has got if he happens to strike a bad day, but when betting with the handbook he bets that much and then stops there, but it is the race-track that gets the bunch of them.
Q. Take the man who follows the races, who bets on the horses, does he usually begin by betting with the book-maker on the track or betting with the hand-book man up town; where does he usually begin his betting career?-A. Usually at the track he starts.
Q. You have no doubt as to that?-A. No, sir.
Again he said:
Q. The large number of persons you have spoken of as having ruined themselves, as having suffered the loss of their business and so on, would they in your opinion have suffered those losses and ruined their lives to the extent they did, had it not been for the book-maker?

A. No, I don't think they Would have. No, they would not. They lost it on the track practically.
Again speaking of the comparatively greater evils resulting from betting on the track, he said:
A man goes to the track, he takes his wad down with him, and if he loses $10 on the first race he tries to make it up on the next race, and if he loses it on the second race he , tries to make it up again on the third, and before he goes back he is broke. But on the hand-book they aint got that chance to do it.
There we have the evidence of Detective Duncan and Inspector Archibald and this man Batt, who has had great experience on the race-track, and their evidence is to the effect that the evil resulting from book-making on the track is infinitely greater than what results from the hand-book men up town. I was talking to one of the leading criminal lawvers in Toronto, and he told me that whatever knowledge he had gained of Tace-track betting was from his defending criminals in Toronto, and he told me that if I could get this legislation on the statute-book, I would accomplish a great deal of good. Can any one doubt that young men do not learn
to bet and become addicted to betting on horse-racing with the hand-book men up town, but with the book-makers on the track? I have always known it to be the case that the opponents of a Bill, when they cannot meet the argument squarely; when they cannot defeat the measure on its merits, will say that it does not go far enough, that there are loop holes in it, and that it will not have the results intended. And so, they sav. if this Bill becomes law, there wili be the private bettor in disguise. Mr. Orpen, giving his evidence, said-page 123-that the interpretation the courts had giveu to the present law, that the book-keener must keep moving about, has so injured the business of the book-maker that he himself has gone out of the business and that it is impossible to carry on the business with anything like the' profit, that was possible before that interpretation was placed on the law. I argue that if the present interpretation of the existing law has driven Mr. Orpen as a book-maker out of the business there would be no possibility at all of the book-maker plying his calling as a disguised private bettor under this measure. Inspector Duncan was asked questions as reported at pages 203-4:
In most of the cases that you have spoken of, and most of the cases that have come to your knowledge, have most of them been the result of betting with book-makers, or have they been the result of private bets?-A. With the book-maker op the race-track or the hand-book man up town.
Q. In almost every instance that has been the case?-A. Yes.
And Detective Sleeman-page 377:
Q. Do not let us quarrel or quibble. If you do away with the book-maker, and there must be betting, with whom is the man going to bet?-A. I do not think we will have very much betting if the book-maker is done away with.
That is the evidence of an experienced detective of the highest standing. I want to give the House now the opinion of Mr. Counsell, one. of the solicitors who appeared in opposition to the Bill, a gentleman of high standing at the bar in the city of Hamilton, Ontario. And I desire to say that I agree with what appears to be his opinion. He said in questioning Mr. Batt:
Q. There is just one question I want to ask about betting by individuals; there is very little betting by individuals on the racetrack, is there?-A. A man that wants to bet bets with the book-maker, there is practically no individual betting at the race-track.
Q. The betting is done with the book-maker ? -A. Yes, it is ivith the book-maker.
And now he says-and it is in this that I agree with him:

Q. You and I cannot make a bet very well without the book-maker at a horse race?-A. Not very well, no.
I agree with Mr. Counsell and Mr. Batt, from the knowledge I have been able to obtain, that if you take away the bookmaker you take away largely the possibility of extensive betting. Mr. C. J. Smith also gave evidence. I may explain that Mr. C. J. Smith is a son of the late joint proprietor in the partnership of Cooper & Smith, wholesale boot and shoe dealers, of Toronto. Mr. Smith stated that he had had large experience as a breeder of race-horses, and as a racing man. His evidence, as it appears at page 451 is as follows:
Q. If a law were passed in Canada to prevent book-making, with that object in view, and if that law were enforced to its full extent as it could reasonably be enforced, could there be any extensive amount of betting going on, on the track with book-makers in disguise who were endeavouring to evade the law?-A. No.
Q. It could not he, it would not be possible? -A. No, no doubt there would be a limited amount, but it would be very small.
Q. Take, for instance, a bank clerk, who was attracted to the race-track through his love of excitement or his love perhaps for horses, would these book-makers in disguise who were endeavouring to evade the law offer to that young man the same temptation to bet on the races as is now offered by book-makers carrying on their business openly?-A. I do not think so, I do not see how it could.
Mr. Penderton was a witness subpoenaed to give evidence in opposition to the Bill. He is, I understand, a detective of large experience, and head of the Thiel Detective Agency of Montreal, an agency well known throughout the United States and Canada. Mr. Meredith asked him:
Q. In your experience at present the average person that bets on the race-course today, does he bet with individuals, or doesn't he bet with the book-makers in preference to betting with the individual?-A. He bets witb the book-maker in preference.
Q. If those book-makers are done away with the parties he will bet with will be the individuals?-A. I do not know who he will bet with and he will find that he does not know either, when he wins.
He, in effect, said that if the professional bettor were there in disguise as a private individual still endeavouring to carry on his business as a book-maker, he would not be there to pay a debt when he lost. How long will men continue to bet with those whom they do not know, and whom they cannot find when they come to claim the payment of a bet?
Another proposition has been made and argued for very earnestly, and that is that we should pass legislation allowing betting with the .book-maker on the" race-Mr. MILLER.
course during the meet, but shortening the length of the meet, confining it, perhaps, to ten or twelve days. In the first place, I desire to read to the House the opinion of the Minister of Justice given in a letter to myself as chairman of the committee, as follows:
Ottawa, February 5, 1910.
Dear Mr. Miller,-I have your letter of the 2nd instant, asking whether the Dominion Parliament has any authority to restrict, or limit, the length of a racing meeting on the tracks of an association incorporated by a provincial legislature.
I think the rational way of regulating such a subject would he by action on the part of the provincial authorities. Such a question seems to me properly a matter of police supervision, and in that view within the jurisdiction of the local authorities. There is nothing I can see to prevent any provincial legislature from requiring licenses to he obtained for the holding of race-track meetings. Under such licenses, they could regulate the days and times that racing could be carried on, charging such license fee as they saw fit. The Dominion parliament has no such jurisdiction, and the only way in which the Dominion parliament could deal with the subject is by undertaking to make it a crime to continue a race-track meeting for more than some given number of days.
I do not question the power of the Dominion parliament to legislate in that majpner, hut it would certainly seem to me entirely illogical to do so. It would be an equivalent to declaring that racing for, say, 30 days was perfectly lawful and innocent, hut that to race on the 31st day was a crime! That does not strike me as sensible or reasonable, and although I think the Dominion parliament has, in its general jurisdiction over criminal law, power to pass such an enactment, it would seem to me that the regulating of the times and manner of conducting race-track meetings was properly a matter for purely provincial attention.
I remain, yours faithfully,
Will the hon. member (Mr. Miller) say why he does not take this agitation to that field?

Because this is one matter, and only one matter, that might be controlled by the provincial legislature. But endeavour to cope with the whole matter and that which we must admit can only be controlled, and ought to be controlled in the Dominion parliament and under the Criminal Code. I think we all agree with the opinion given by the Minister of Justice that it would be within the power of this parliament to enact that racing for thirty days was perfectly lawful, and innocent, but to race on the 31st day was a crime, but we would also agree when he says: ' that does not strike me as sensible or reasonable '. I wish to put the other line of reasoning on a parallel with that and

ask the members of this House whether the position is not very much the same as to say that the Dominion parliament has the power to say that racing is punishable when carried on outside the race-track enclosure, but is innocent, harmless, and no crime if carried on inside the fence that surrounds the race-track. But even if we ^had not the opinion given by the Minister of Justice, we have that of the Hon. Mr. Fisher, who was asked what, in his opinion, would be the effect of shortening the race-meeting to ten days, and he said:
I should think they would be intensified for the. ten days.
Q. In other words, you think they would try to get in the ten days the evil that they had committed in the sixty?-A. I should think
so.
Q. And you do not see any difference between a ten days' and a sixty days' meet in that respect?-A. I think, probably, they could not do as much damage in ten days as they could in sixty days, although they would do as much of their works as they could do in ten.
The Hon. Mr. Templeman was asked his opinion as to limiting the race meeting to ten days, or to any number of days and his reply was: __
I do not believe that if the race-meeting was limited to ten days, and there is bookmaking even to the extent that it might take place in the ten days, that it would meet public opinion in the city of Victoria.
Q- Vou do not think it will?-A. I do not think so. If there is book-making that will permit bank clerks and even young lads to take part in the pools and spend more money than they should, you will never satisfy public opinion.
Now our opponents, with deep concern, tell us that it will be impossible to enforce this legislation, that you cannot enforce the law even though it be the law. I do not know really whether the law could be be enforced or not and again I appeal to Inspector Duncan. In answer to Mr. Moss, page 199, he says:
Q. But you do not expect, as a practical man, to stamp that out by legislation, do you? A. If you want to stamp it out what will you stamp it out with, if you do not get legislation ?
Q. Do you agree with him (Mr. Grasset), that you do not think it can be done away with by Act of parliament?-A. I think it can be done away with.
Q. You think it can?-A. I think it can; you will not eliminate it entirely, but you will get it under control and save a great many people from being ruined.
Then Inspector Archibald, page 226, testified:
Q. Then, if you had a law that was in plain Anglo-Saxon and easy to understand, forbidding betting on the race-tracks through the
book-maker, would it be possible to reasonably enforce that law?-A. Yes.
Q. And suppress the betting?-A. Yes.
Then Detective Sleeman testified:
Q. I am asking you whether, if parliament passed a law making it illegal to bet in any manner, you think, as an experienced officer, that such a law could be successfully enforced ?
I would like to have your candid opinion on that.-A. I think we can. If you give us a law T think there is material enough in the police court and detectives of the Dominion to stamp out the evil spoken of.
Then Detective Carrington, who was brought to give evidence in opposition to the Bill, was asked this question:
Q. Is it difficult to enforce it?-A. Well, I do not think it is difficult, speaking from a professional point of view, to enforce any law if you occupy the position with proper officers.
Detective McMahon testifies:
Q. Do you see any difficulty about enforcing the law against book-making on the racetrack?-A. You can enforce the law to prohibit it, sure.
Now, we have been told that public opinion is not behind this Bill, and that in the absence of public opinion, the law cannot be enforced. On this subject the Hon. Mr. Templeman was asked by Mr. Blain, M. P.:
Q. Would public opinion in the west endorse this Bill?-A. I think it would.
Now, Sir, I will come to the Vancouver Board of Trade. The Vancouver Board of Trade is not made up of parsons, or of men engaged in moral reform movements, but of hard-headed business men, having in view their own interests and the interests of the city, and this is the resolution they passed on the 5th of last November:
The Right Honourable the Minister of Justice, Ottawa.
Sir,-I have the honour to advise you that-
Whereas, the question of race-track gambling in connection with the recently established 'Minoru Race Track' on Lulu island near the city, was fully discussed at the monthly meeting of this board on 5th October ultimo;
Whereas, the opinion was unanimous that in relation to the welfare and business interests of the city and of the community at large, legislation should be sought to effect the suppression of all professional gambling on race-tracks;
Whereas, the hoard is advised by the attorney general of British Columbia ' That the question of the suppression of gambling is one coming entirely within the powers of the Dominion parliament;
It was resolved, at a meeting of the council board held on the 4th inst. That the hon. the Minister of Justice be requested to adopt such legislation as may be necessary to bring the

suppression of race-track gambling within the Criminal Code of Canada.
I have the honour to be,
Your obedient servant,

Secretary.
Mr. Cowan, member of parliament for Vancouver, gave his opinion:
Q. Well, will public opinion in your province endorse this Bill as it now stands, do you think?-A. I scarcely know how it stands.
Q. Supposing it does all we say it does?- A. That it does away with the book-maker?
Q. It does away entirely with the bookmaker?-A. Yes, it will endorse it.
Then Mr. Cowan went further, and said:
Q. I merely wish to let the committee know the status of these gentlemen?-A. I know that not only the directors but the shareholders of this association are beyond criticism, substantial men, men who would not be identified with anything of a doubtful character if they knew it.
Q. Bo they approve of this Bill?-A. I imagine that the majority of them do.
So we have the statement of a member of this House that the men who compose the Vancouver Racing Association are in favour of this Bill, and will support it. Inspector Archibald again testifies:
Q. You are in a very good position to have some knowledge of what is public opinion on this very question: if there should be a law passed now to entirely prohibit race-track gambling through the book-maker, do you think there is a public opinion that would assist you in enforcing that law?-A. I am very strongly of the opinion that there is already that public opinion.
Mr. Moss asked Detective Sleeman this question:	.
Q. You think you can stamp it out altogether?-A. I will do my part.
Q. Bo you think the community will acquiesce in that?-A. I think you would have the community with you if you would stop book-making.
Now, Sir, let us no longer ask whether there is or is not public opinion behind this Bill, because the evidence is very clear that there is. Mr. E. C. Drury, master of the Dominion Grange, says:
I am fullv convinced that popular feeling among the farmers stands behind Mr. Miller's Bill.
Let me point out to you also, Mr. Speaker, that all the church papers of Canada are strongly in favour of the Bill. The Toronto ' Globe,' the Toronto ' Telegram,' the Toronto ' Star, the Canadian ' Courier,' the Canadian ' Collier's,' and the local press throughout Canada, and most significant of all, all the farm papers and live stock journals have expressed themselves as being entirely in sympathy with the Bill now before the House. And last, but not least let me say that the Orange Lodge of Mr. MILLER
Canada, in session recently, expressed itself very strongly in favour of the Bill; and no other resolution passed at the meeting of the Grand Lodge was so unanimously and so enthusiastically supported as was a resolution favouring this Bill. Now, Sir, why should there not be public opinion behind this Bill?
We have had similar legislation in the state of New York, in the state of Michigan, in nearly all the leading horse-breeding states of the American union. With a larger and longer experience than we have had, they have passed legislation prohibiting race-track gambling in those states. I do not say that in legislation, along the line of moral reform or otherwise, we should always follow their example, but I say that in legislating along these lines we have usually supposed ourselves to be at least up to as high a standard as the citizens of the United States, and I ask whether it is to be tolerated, whether it is to be supposed that we will continue to make Canada a dumping ground for the professional gamblers of the race-track banished by this legislation from the racetracks of the American union. It has been said that we ought to follow English precedent, and that in place of that we* are in this legislation seeking to follow American precedent. Let us see whether we have any precedent in following American rather than English precedent. At page 563-4 of the evidence, Mr. Nelson, sporting editor of the Toronto ' Globe ', in replying to Mr. McCarthy explained the English system. He said that the system at the English race-tracks is that the book-maker is not allowed to be at the grand stand, or in the ground with the ordinary attendants at the races. The book-maker is shut off in a pen or inclosure for admission to which he pays a £1 entrance fee. The ordinary attendants at the races do not come in contact with the book-maker at all; if they want to get in contact with him in his inclosure they also must pay an additional £1. This is in itself a great protection to the young men of Great Britain, and to men who have not become addicted to racetrack gambling. Mr. Blain asked Mr. Nelson:
Do you think that would be a desirable change for Canada?
And Mr. Nelson's reply was:
No sir.
The chairman said:
You do not believe, then, that in all things we should follow the English practice?
And Mr. Nehon's reply was:
No.
If the men who carry on the races persist in following not the English, not the

British, but the American system, they cannot, I think, find fault with us if we endeavour to meet the conditions they make with legislation more similar to that of America, than to that of Britain.
In conclusion, it has been said that Dr. Shearer has been at the bottom of all this agitation, that the legislation is really his legislation, that this whole matter has come from the agitation of preachers and pastors. I wish to read from the argument of the counsel opposed to this Bill. At page 9 they say:
The undersigned do not desire to cast any reflection upon the many excellent and eminent ministers of the church who have been induced to lend their names to the agitation fostered by Dr. Shearer, nor to minimize the service they can do the community in uplifting its moral tone by exhortation and example, but ft is respectfully urged that the promotion of legislation forms no part of the professional duty of a minister of the gospel.
Note the argument and turn to page 49 of the same argument where you will see:
The supporters of the Bill have tried to lay stress on the fact that some of the racing clubs derive an income from the sale of telegraphic information in regard to the racing and betting. There is no law prohibiting the sale of this information, and it is quite natural that the clubs should sell it if some one is willing to pay for it, and if they did not do so, the information would be obtained notwithstanding.
We have the statements of the opponents of the Bill that they have been selling information from their race-tracks for the carrying on and maintenance of pool-rooms in the United States, and in distant cities. They admit that it is not a right thing to do, and they say they do not want to be longer permitted to do it, but are willing to abandon it, as a thing that ought not to be continued. But how long would it have taken the appeals and exhortations of ministers to prevent these men from continuing to sell racing information? It was only the prospect of legislation that made them abandon this, as they are now ready to do. How long would it take these men to be influenced in any degree by the example and exhortation of ministers? I am prepared to admit that no minister or pastor ought to endeavour to or be permitted to dictate as to what shall be the legislation of this House; but I do contend that it is the right of a minister of the gospel to suggest legislation. Men supporting this Bill have been accused of being narrowminded. I have myself been accused of being narrow-minded in supporting this Bill, as have many others. Can there be any greater evidence of a narrow mind than this, that a man when asked to support a Bill will say:	In whose brain did
that Bill originate, in whose brain was it
formed? Then, if it is the suggestion of a minister: I will not support it. If it is the suggestion of some other man: I will. Is that a broad way to look at legislation? Will not the broad-minded man say: If this Bill is reasonable and right I will support it, if it is wrong I will oppose it no matter whence it comes? No minister has ever endeavoured to control my course in any legislation, and no minister of the gospel need try, because no minister can.
I would not ask any member to vote on this or on any question as he may have been dictated to by any one. I have not seen any evidence that any minister of the gospel has endeavoured to dictate to any member how he shall vote. It has been said that the public opinion in favour of the Bill is largely the result of petitions and circulars. The repeal of the Corn laws in Great Britain, the reform law of 1832, the emancipation of the Catholics, all these great reforms were the result of long-continued agitation, and arguments, public meetings, the agitation of the public mind in every possible way, and in that way they were carried. In that way all such legislation, and all great reforms have been brought about and carried. It has been said that you cannot make men good by Act of parliament. It was a saying of Mr. Gladstone-that it is the duty of parliament to make it as easy as possible for men to do right, and as difficult as possible for men to do wrong.
I have been glad to see the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) who is chairman of the Conservation Commission taking notes, and I assume he will speak on this subject. I have no knowledge nor is it any business of mine whether he will speak in favour of, or against the Bill; but as a great Canadian, as a man who has taken a great interest in the conserving of our natural resources, I cannot believe he will fail to realize that the greatest natural resources we have are Canadian men and women. I cannot but believe that the chairman of that Conservation Commission, who endeavours to protect the water-powers of Canada, will realize that the greatest power Canada has is the power of Canadian men and Canadian women. I cannot but believe that the chairman of that commission, who endeavours to preserve the small trees in our forests, will endeavour to preserve to Canada the small boys, the young men of Canada. I cannot but believe that the chairman of that commission, who endeavours to protect for Canada, gold, coal, iron, and all the ores that exist in the country, will endeavour to protect the gold in the pockets of Canada, and not permit it to be taken away by American book-makers who invade our land. I cannot believe that the chairman of the Conservation Commission who says

that no American shall interfere with our waterways will permit a herd of American book-makers to control our race-tracks in Canada, and deteriorate the morals, and take away the character, the reputation, and the respectability of the Canadian people. The names of people in high places whom the rules of parliament prevent me from mentioning have been invoked in this debate; their practices have- been quoted by the opponents of the Bill. I say, Sir, that is hardly fair to gentlemen who occupy places of high position m the land, because these gentlemen on account of their position cannot reply to the statements made. I may say, Sir, that a certain gentleman in England occupying the highest position; one who is sometimes referred to as the first gentleman of Britain wrote a letter a little while ago on this question of gambling, and that letter is reported in the Toronto ' Star,' of February 24. The item says that the Reverend Montague Fowler, lecturing on the subject of racing, and gambling quoted the following from a letter written by this high personage:
I have horror of gambling and shall always do my utmost to discourage others who have an inclination for it, as the spirit of gambling like intemperance is one of the greatest evils than can afflict a country.
I am not by the rules of the House permitted to mention the name of the person who wrote that letter, but I do say that when that personage writes that gambling is one of the greatest evils that can afflict a country, we cannot be found fault with by that gentleman or by the gentleman who represents him in Canada or by any others who are loyal British subjects if we support this Bill.
In conclusion I may say that when we get into committee to deal with the Bill section by section, I shall offer amendments that will make it perfectly clear that section 227 does not relate to bets between private individuals and which will make less drastic the provisions of section 235 as to the publication of racing information.

McCOLL (Northumberland, Ont. W. R.) My hon. friend (Mr. Miller) has referred to what he calls the opponents of this Bill. Mr. Speaker, there are no oppo-ments to the general principle of the Bill. There are no opponents to the leading features of this Bill, but there are opponents to the drastic, extreme, unjust, and unfair provisions of this Bill. Now, what is the general principle of this Bill? The general principle of the Bill is to amend the Criminal Code in such a manner as to make the law more effective in restricting and abolishing gambling and the evils resulting therefrom, and particularly that class of gambling known as race-track gambling. And, what are the leading features and pro- 1 Mr. MILLER.
visions of this Bill? The leading features and provisions of the Bill are to broaden and extend the definition of common gaming house, common betting house, and disorderly houses to make the law more effective in abolishing that class of gambling carried on by means of what are known as hand-books or hand-book operators; to abolish what are known as toots and tipsters and the operations carried on by such persons; to abolish the sale of tips, the sale of racing information publishing odds on races, and the advertising of racing information. Now, what are the drastic ahd extreme and unjust and unfair provisions of the Bill? This proposed legislation invokes the Criminal Code and makes criminal certain acts and courses of conduct which a large portion of the public, perhaps the large majority of the people of Canada, look upon as absolutely a harmless and innocent recreation. Any such legislation I submit is drastic and extreme. This proposed legislation in its present form, according to the overwhelming weight of evidence presented to the committee will seriously affect if not totally abolish the noble and royal sport of horse-racing; a sport that has been fostered, encouraged, promoted, and patronized by the kings of England for the last 200 years, and which is being encouraged and promoted and patronized today not only by the present King of Great Britain but by other crowned heads and governments of Europe. I submit that any legislation that will seriously interfere with or abolish such a sport is drastic and extreme. Then, according to the evidence submitted to the Committee the Bill in its present form would certainly affect the light horse-breeding in Canada and the result in great financial loss to the importers and producers of the thoroughbred, standard breed, and other light horse breeds of Canada by depreciating the value of their stables and business. I submit, Sir, that any legislation having that result is unjust and unfair. Then, according to the evidence the Bill if passed in its present form would cause great financial loss to the jockey clubs and other racing associations by depreciating the value of their properties and plants. Therefore the features of the Bill in that respect are unjust as unfair.
Now Mr. Speaker my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) quoted from the evidence to show that the real issue between what he calls the opponents of the Bill and the promoters of the Bill was narrowed down to a very fine point. In fact he quoted from the evidence to show that the so called opponents of the Bill were ready and willing to cooperate, and I may say they did co-operate with the promoters of the Bill in amending the Bill so as to greatly improve on its original form. Then, the only point of difference between the promoters of the Bill

and the so-called opponents of the Bill is this: That the promoters of the Bill desire to abolish absolutely all kinds of public betting on a race-course while the race is in actual progress; and the so-called opponents of the Bill desire to protect the racing, by permitting, as has always been permitted in Canada, the privilege of betting upon the race-course during the actual progress of the race meeting. Now Sir, my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) in the course of his remarks frequently used the expression ' race-track gambling,' and it appeared to me as if he liked to use that expression as often as possible. I am going to argue Sir, that what takes place on a well regulated race-course such as some of the racecourses we have in Canada is not race track gambling, and that the evils admitted on all hands which do result from race-track gambling do not occur upon the race-courses, but outside of the race-track altogether. When I am arguing in favour of race-track associations or jockey clubs, I mean those conducted by the class of men who are in that business for the sport that is in it, and not race-tracks that are conducted purely for business purposes or perhaps for gambling purposes. In this connection I wish to quote a statement made bv Mr. Raney, solicitor for the promoters of the Bill, made at the beginning of the proceedings and before any evidence was taken. It will be found at pages 7 and 8 of the proceedings. He said:-
There is a broad line of demarcation separating these tracks into two classes, and I may classify them in this way: on the one side of the line are the Woodbine, the Montreal track and the Hamilton track. On the other side of the line of demarcation are the Fort Erie track, the Windsor track, the British Columbia track. These tracks are divided, as I say, by a line of demarcation, and I will define at once what that line of demarcation is. To illustrate it, I will refer to two tracks-the Woodbine on the one side and the Fort Erie on the other as types of these two classes. Now the Woodbine race meet is essentially a social and a sporting event; attracting many of the best people of Canada, with race-track book-making as an attraction and as a principal financial support. This race-track is managed as you have heard from Mr. McCarthy, by eminently respectable men, strong men financially, all Canadians.
It is the class of race-track which Mr. Raney has there described that the so-called opponents of this Bill desire to protect. What I say is this-and I speak not only from the overwhelming evidence that has been brought before the committee, but also from personal knowledge of what I have seen and observed on the Woodbine Tace-course at	Toronto-that
practically all the betting that goes on there is not gambling in the strict sense of the word. What is it? In tbe first
place, I will refer to my own riding, and I will ask every other member of the House also to bring his mind to bear on what exists in his own constituency-the class of people in his constituency who go to the Woodbine or any other race-track of the class I have described, and say whether or not he would consider them to be gamblers in any sense of the word. Probably not more than a dozen, or twenty at the outside, of my constituents ever go to a race-track where book-making or pool-selling takes place. These men are not gamblers in any sense of the word. I can recall two of them who do not even know how to play a game of cards, who do not bet on hockey matches, baseball or prize fighting. These men go to the Woodbine ; they look forward to spending a day or two there during the year for the sport and recreation they get. While there they bet. They may bet $2 or $5 on a race. Generally six or seven races take place in a day. They may win or they may lose. As a result, they may be $10 or $20 ahead or they may be that much behind. But, whether they lose or not, they have enjoyed their sport, they have had their outing. That is the form of recreation they take. They are not injured by it in any way, and to call these men gamblers would be absolutely wrong. With regard to the betting that takes place there, whether it is right or wrong, it is something that has grown up among the British people and has been going on for centuries. It is an incident of the great national sport of horse-racing that betting takes nlace on the results. The betting is an incident to the sport. Probably 90 per cent of the people who go to a race meeting conducted as the Woodbine is, and bet at all, are of that class of people. They bet as an incident of the sport, not with the gambling instinct at all. It has been said that if we abolish book-making and public betting on the race-track, it will not interfere with racing. But one of the proofs that the betting privileges are a great attraction for those who go to race meetings to enjoy the sport is that if these are removed, the attendance falls off, the races are not patronized, the gate receipts go, and the whole thing eventually fails altogether. To take the other side for a moment, I may be asked, do you pretend to argue that there are no evils resulting from race-track gambling? Certainly, very many evils have grown up from race-track gambling. What are 'they? What takes place in the pool rooms and on the streets? What takes place by the operation of handbooks, in barber shops, in third-rate hotels, in butcher shops, and so on? We had it clearly demonstrated before the committee that in the city of Toronto to-day there are probably from 300 to 500 hand-book

operators. How do they operate? What do they bet on? There are no races going on in Toronto to-day. Their betting is done on race-meets which are going on in the United States-at Jacksonville, Tampa, Oakland, California, and so on. How is that done? By means of reading the newspapers. In the early morning they see the entries that have been made for the races at Jacksonville in the afternoon, and there is thus an opportunity for them to go out and make their bets. They go around canvassing people on th*. streets. They canvass workmen, even going to the Massey-Harris factory, and make bets of from 25 cents to $2, or even more. How do they decide the bet ? The next morning the reports come out in the newspapers showing what horses won and the odds against them, and those who risked their money, are paid off according to the published results. The unanimous opinion of the committee was that it was highly desirable to abolish all that class of gambling, which is going on from day to day in the way I| have described. That is what can bei termed strictly race-track gambling. WhatJ I have described as taking place at a well; conducted race-meet is not race-track gambling, but an act which is an incident and an incentive to horse-racing.
My hon. friend has tried to impress upon the House the idea that book-makers are very undesirable men, whose principal business is to rob the public. Let us be just and consider for a moment what bookmaking really is and how it is carried on. This Bill aims at prohibiting pool-selling and book-making. What is pool-selling? That is something which is practised principally at trotting meets, but at running meets of the various jockey clubs, bookmaking takes the place of pool-selling. At the trotting meets both are carried on, but it is chiefly the pool-seller who operates. What are his operations? He acts as an agent for the public who desire to bet. He sells the pools and takes in the cash, and when the race is over, he deducts his five or ten per cent, and the rest of the money is divided among the winners. So that what money the pool-seller takes in goes back to the public, less the commission which he charges. The book-maker, who carries on his legitimate business, is in exactly the same position. His position is as close to that of a stock-broker as you can imagine. That was the general tenor of the evidence before the committee. Poolselling appears to jbe a very satisfactory way of betting at a trotting race. There you would probably have two races in the afternoon.. The races are run in heats, the best two out of three or three out of five. At running meets, however, the contests are all dash races, there may be six or seven a day, and an entirelv different class of horses come out in each race. Pool-Mr. McCOLL.
selling is, therefore, not a convenient or satisfactory way of betting at such meets, the book-maker consequently takes the place of the pool-seller. I might just mention that a book-maker on a race-track of an association such as the Woodbine is a different man altogether from the bookmaker who may operate in a pool-room or upon that other "class of tracks to which I shall refer later. The book-maker on tracks such as the Woodbine are under regulations. Every precaution is taken to protect the public, and they almost invariably stick to their legitimate business, which is this: The book-maker takes the horses which are to start in a certain race and puts up their names on a blackboard. He then gives the odds-one at even money, another at two to three, and so on. Under ordinary circumstances the book-maker- it is a mathematical calculation-ought to make ten or five per cent profit out of his operations, just the same as the pool-seller does. His calculations may go wrong. On one race he may lose and not make any percentage; on the next he may win. But if he carries on his legitimate business, he starts on a basis of making five or ten per cent, and on the average he does so. But if he should step outside legitimate business and go into speculating himself, he may win or lose, just the same as any other speculator. It is the public who really make the odds. You will continually see the slate changing. A horse quoted at one price may be quoted at an entirely different price in another minute. It all depends on how the public bet. The bookmaker, in order to protect himself, has to change the odds, and his object is to take in something on every horse. There may be ten in the race. He has a better chance to come out even on the ten, because if all the public bet on the one horse, and that horse won, the book-maker would be broke. Every book-maker on a well regulated track is nothing more than an agent of the public^ doing business in the way I have described. He is not that terrible individual which many people, who know nothing about the subject, imagine him to be, or my hon. friend would have the House believe he is.
What further do we see at the Woodbine? Every precaution is taken to protect the public. It is well provided with police. The local Toronto force is there, and in addition, special Pinkerton men are engaged at the expense of the club. These men appear on the course in plain clothes. They collect information and report to the local police, so that if the police see any parties who are undesirable, these parties are at once dealt with. What I am stating appears in the evidence taken before the committee, and I do not propose to take up time by quoting page after page of that evidence.

Again, we find that before the race-meet takes place, the authorities are in communication with the Pinkerton or other detective agencies, which they require to be on the lookout for any undesirable class of people about to leave Chicago or New York or Chicago, or elsewhere, for Toronto. The local force is on the lookout for just such people as soon as they arrive. If these suspects turn out not to be too hard looking, they aTe allowed to go free on condition that they leave town; but if they are considered too dangerous to let go, they are kept in custody until the meet is over. These are things that are done, these are provisions that are made, to protect the public against the undesirable classes that are likely to come to any large gathering. According to the evidence before the committee, there are far more offences in the way of pickpocketing and such like at the Toronto exhibition than at the Woodbine. As I say. there is an undesirable class, pickpockets, thieves and fakirs of different kinds, that are attracted to every large gathering.
They follow every crowd.

Yes. So long as horse-Tacing continues, that class will endeavour to get there, and the most that any racing association can do is to take the greatest precautions to protect the public against them. That is done, and done at great expense, at the Woodbine. Again, they protect the public in the matter of betting in this way: A race-horse owner comes there with his stable. He has a good horse. The horse starts on the opening day, and the public, knowing it from reputation, bet their money on it. But he shows poor form, makes a bad showing and the people lose their money. A day or two afterwards, the same horse appears and. there is a great reversal of form, but the public, thinking that the horse is out of form do not bet on him, he is a long price in the books; but that day he goes out and wins. If that occurs at the Woodbine, what is done? The owner and trainer are at once brought before the stewards at the jockey club, and if the owner cannot give a satisfactory explanation-sometimes there may be a satisfactory explanation, for the horse may have been interfered with in the race or may not be in proper form- but, unless the explanation is satisfactory, that man is ruled off the course, he and his stable, ejected from the Woodbine and not permitted to race there any longer. That is another means that the club takes to protect the public. It sometimes happens that the jockeys may be bribed to pull a horse or to do something wrong in that regard. That very Tarelv happens, if it happens at all, at a well conducted race-track, such as the Woodbine. Ami why? These jockeys are licensed, they
are paid large salaries, their business is like a profession, and if they are found doing anything wrong or crooked, they are at once brought before the stewards, their licenses are cancelled and their business is taken from them. I might mention other ways in which a race-track such as the Woodbine takes every means in its power to protect the public.
There are, however, race-tracks of another class. I do not know whether they exist in Canada or not. It appears from the evidence before the committee that Fort Erie and Windsor at one time were objectionable, but they are not so now. But, if there is anything wrong at any racetrack, I submit that that is a matter for regulation and not for invoking the Criminal Code. Why should the men at the head of Tacing associations and jockey clubs such as I have described be brought before the public as criminals, or as consorting with criminals, when these meets could be regulated by the proper authorities? If we have not the jurisdiction, then go to the authority that has the jurisdiction and ask for regulation, but do not take the drastic means of invoking the Criminal Code. Reference has been made to the Vancouver race-meet that took place last year. That was an exceptional case, and, in dealing with it, I will give the substance of the evidence before the committee. It appears that men interested in the racing business organized a racing association at Vancouver and built a new race-track which they named the Minoru after King Edward's Derby winner of last year. Instead of operating the track last year, they rented it to an American concern, and, unfortunately, rented it for sixty days or ninety days-I have forgotten the number. Last year, a fair was .going on at Seattle which brought large crowds of people to that city. It appears that there are boats plying regularly between Seattle and Vancouver. Extra boats were put on to take the crowds to this race meet, and, according to the evidence before the corn-mitte-e, a disgraceful state of affairs existed there, something that should be entirely prohibited, something that no one would justify. The local authorities could have stopped it-so it appeared from the evidence before the committee-had they seen fit to do so; they could have cancelled the contract they had with the Americans. That probably would have meant an action for damages, and _ the payment of money which, it is to be supposed,	they	did not	wish	to
be called upon to pay. It will be seen that there were special circumstances there that are not likely to occur again, and the concurrence of which could be prevented by action of the local authorities. I see it stated in the public press that the muni-

cipal authorities of Victoria have already taken steps to prevent occurrences similar to those of last year. So, if there be objectionable race-tracks, there is a means of regulating them, otherwise than by invoking the Criminal Code as proposed under this Bill.
Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) quoted a great deal of the evidence and referred to a number of witnesses. But, I think that if you will read the evidence of these several witnesses that he quoted-read the whole of their evidence-you will find that my hon. friend, perhaps, was not entirely fair in the impression that he tried to give to the House of that evidence. Again, it would appear to me to be only a proper thing, if he wished to be fair in laying the matter before the House, to give both-sides, if there be two sides to it. He quoted the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) and tried to give great weight to the evidence given by that gentleman. But read the evidence of the Minister of Agriculture and you will find that he admitted that he practically knew nothing about the thing at all. I draw the attention of the House to the fact that the Minister of Agriculture has not yet established a racing branch in connection with his department. As against the evidence given by the Minister of Agriculture. I will refer to that of Dr. Rutherford. Dr. Rutherford also was quoted by my hon. friend; but I ask any hon. member of the House to read the whole of Dr. Rutherford's evidence. In the first place, before he became a veterinary director general, he managed a large racing-stable in the United States. Besides, he was a breeder of thoroughbreds. He spoke from a personal knowledge of the racing business for years. Read his evidence in full. That evidence clearly establishes, in the first place, that the thoroughbred is a very important, probably the most important, breed of horses in the world to-day. It is established that the thoroughbred is the foundation of all the light horses of the country, that the thoroughbred is used in improving the hackney, the standard breed of all the different classes of light horses in Canada. It is also established in Dr. Rutherford's evidence that racing is necessary to develop the thoroughbred, to develop his intelligence, his courage, his stamina and so on. Let me say that witness upon witness came before the committee giving _ evidence along the same lines, and establishing that the thoroughbred was very necessary for the breeding industry of the country, that racing was necessary to develop that horse, and that in order to promote racing it was necessary to have some kind of public betting on the racecourse. and thaMf that were abolished, not only would racing deteriorate, but would probably die out. Witness after witness testified along these lines, and I appeal to Mr. McCOLL.
any member of the committee, that when it was proposed to bring further witnesses, the committee were unanimously of the opinion that these facts had been fully established, that there was no dispute, and that it was unnecessary for those who were opposing the drastic provisions of the Bill to bring further witnesses. I may mention a few who testified before the committee: We had Dr. Rutherford, we had Mr. Dy-ment, ex-M.P., we had the Hon. J. H. Hen-drie, one of the greatest 'breeders of thoroughbreds in the country, Dr. McEachern, Major Wm. Hendrie, Mr. Yager, of Sim-coe, a breeder of hackneys that he crosses with thoroughbreds. So, when my hon. friend to-day undertook to show that the thoroughbred was absolutely of no use for any purpose -whatever, and I think he went to that extent, I was very much surprised, because that was entirely contrary to the evidence.
Now, my hon. friend has quoted some other authorities. You will remember he quoted from a book of Mr. E. King Dodds, he was for many years editor of the ' Canadian Sportsman.' Those are the head notes to the article written by Mr. Dodds. From that article I quote:
If betting under any and all systems is prohibited oh Canadian race-tracks, the clubs

must either close their gates or offer such small purses that it would be impossible for a horse owner to pay running expenses, even should he win a liberal proportion of the prizes offered. Again:
Mr. Raney's contention is that betting at the track, even during the progress of the racing, is not essential, and that its elimination would not injuriously affect the interests of horse-breedineg.
That is Mr. Raney's contention. Now take Mr. Dodds' comment on that, and the proof he adduces;
Devoid as he is of experience, his opinion on this question is valueless. The so-called Hughes law in the state of New York provides ample testimony to the contrary. Stakes like the Brooklyn and Surburban handicaps, the value of each of which, previous to the passage of that law, -was $25,000, have been cut down, so that in 1909 the value to the winners was only $3,850 in each event. Other stakes previously worth $10,000 were reduced to $2,000, and over-night events of $1,250 and $1,500 have shrunk to $400 and $500, while the attendance of spectators at the Metropolitan meetings fell off from an average of 12,000 to less than 3,000 per day. Such great racing stables as those of Messrs. Belmont, Vanderbilt, Keene, Whitney and others, have been forced to transfer their horses to Great Britain and Prance where wiser laws govern the sport.
My hon. friend read a long list of events that are announced to take place on the New York tracks during the coming season, I think he read 15. But he did not compare the purses given during the coming year with the purses given in the past, and, perhaps, it might be well for me here to refer a little to this Hughes law. Two years ago the law was passed in the state of New York and some other states of the union abolishing betting at racetracks, abolishing the book-maker. What is the result? Has the Act been a success? What do we find this year? There are three Bills before the New York legislature proposing changes in the Hughes law. That law did not abolish gambling as expected, according to the evidence brought before our committee by representatives of the Pinkerton and Thiel detective 'agencies. Assuming that this Bill would have the same effect as the Hughes Bill, what would be the result in Canada? Whereas, now public betting is allowed to book-makers under regulation by the association, if the book-makers were prohibited from going to the track, any betting that took, place would have to be done by private betting, which my hon. friend says is not to be interfered with by this legislation. I have said that the large majority of people who go to the Woodbine or to places of that 205
kind, to a track conducted first for the sport, go there and bet from a sporting instinct and not from a gambling instinct. But when there is a chance to bet, gamblers bet with the book-makers and among themselvea Abolish the book-maker. Then the gambling element would go there just as before, but while they used to bet with the book-makers, they would have to find some one else to bet with. They would be able to say they were only private betters, that they were not making books, and that under the law they were legalized and recognized. In Toronto or New York all that gambling element who would go down and bet with the book-maker under present conditions would go there and bet in their private capacity, taking in as many of the other visitors to the races as tney possibly could. We will suppose that a man goes to the race-track to enjoy the sport, and that there is no book-maker present. He would like to bet $5 on a race. The promoters of this Bill say that he should find out his friends and bet with them. He may have no friends there. Then they say: give it up altogether. Yes, the man may give it up, but it will be found that there are any number of men of the class I have spoken of, men who may have been objectionable book-makers under other conditions, ready to accommodate him and take his bet. He will then be betting without any protection, and if he wins the chances are he will not get his money. He is betting with strangers, and the result will be that that class of better, that is the sporting element, will not take their chances of betting with strangers, they will keep away from the track, and racing will deteriorate. That will leave a larger field for the regular gambler. They will go down there and bet among themselves or with others, they will bet orally, they will make no books, and the evidence is that that has been the result of the operation of the Hughes law in New York, and that the real evils of gambling have been largely increased rather than diminished by its operation. That in effect is the general result of that law. Racing has been deteriorated, the sporting element who formerly patronized these tracks and their large stables have gone to Europe, to England and France. The other patrons of the track who would go there to enjoy the spoTt keep away, and the race-tracks now are in full control of the gambling element. The pool-rooms in New York have increased largely since the Hughes law went into force. That has been the result, and I think it only fair to assume that it may be the result here if this Bill passes in its present form. If there be any doubt as to whether or not it would have that effect, would it not be better to take no chances on it? The Bill goes very far. It is in-



tended to remove all the admitted evils of race-track gambling. Then it appears to me it would be wisdom all round not to go too far, but to concede the small provisions that the so-called opponents of the Bill desire. In that way we would be protecting the sporting interests, we would be protecting horse-breeding in Canada, and we would not be inflicting serious injury on any one.
Another question to which my hon. friend referred was the economic question. He stated that the jockey clubs and racing associations obtained large revenues from the sale of book-making privileges. That is quite true, but if this legislation goes into force, as the majority of the committee desire, if all the provisions about which there is no dispute go into force, then they will not have that large revenue, and they will be losing to that extent. My hon. friend tried to lead the House to believe that something like $2,000,000 was taken annually from the people of Canada by book-makers from the United States. That was entirely erroneous. The evidence before the committee was that almost invariably, particularly at the spring meeting at the Woodbine, the book-makers actually lost money. You would say why would they give large sums for the racing privilege if they were losing money by them? The explanation is that as a part of the privileges they get tliey have the right to have a telegraph office at the Woodbine, and to send information on the races to the United States. It appears that there is an association known as the Interstate News Company, whose head office is in New York. As each race is run at the Woodbine, information regarding that race is sent to that Interstate News Company. For instance, you will see alongside of this telegraph office a man with a field glass calling off the horses at their positions at the post and at each quarter pole, The odds that the public make on the racetrack are also telegraphed to that Interstate Association. Then the company telegraph that same information to all the pool-rooms in the United States, so that while the races are actually taking place at the Woodbine, under conditions that have grown up in recent years by allowing that information to go out, a system of gambling that is purely race-track gambling is going on in all the pool-rooms of the United States. But, you say, how do they make their money? This is how. It appeared in the evidence-and that from witnesses brought by the promoters of the Bill-that it was a practice in the poolrooms, where the betting took place, to give just double the odds against the bettor that would be given on tne race-track, so that the book-makers might be losing a large amount of money at the Woodbine, 1 Mr. McCOLL.
and yet in the pool-rooms away from the track, where the odds *were doubled against the bettor, they might be able to make a large amount of money. It is because of that privilege of having telegraph companies upon the race-track sending out the information that they can afford to give the money they do for the betting privileges. All are agreed that that condition of affairs should be stopped. I would here point out that although this practice is of no special injury to Canada, because the gambling takes place in another country, yet it is no doubt an injury to our neighbours to the south of the line, as it enables them to carry on a large system of what is actually and truly race-track gambling, and it would be our duty, I believe, to prohibit that.
As good neighbours.
